posts.title: PACS servers, imaging equipment, and viewers often expose DICOM with little or no authentication. To make these systems easier to audit, I contributed 8 new scripts and a major upg
posts.author: Paulino Calderon
posts.snippet:
PACS servers, imaging equipment, and viewers often expose DICOM with little or no authentication. To make these systems easier to audit, I contributed 8 new scripts and a major upgrade to the dicom.lua library:
 * dicom-info: Fingerprints DICOM servers (implementation UID and version, SOP classes, transfer syntaxes, max PDU size). Over TLS it also checks for weak crypto, self-signed certificates and whether mutual TLS is enforced.
 * dicom-cfind-ls: Runs C-FIND queries to list studies, series and patient metadata. Flags archives that allow unauthenticated queries.
* dicom-cmove: Tests whether stored studies can be sent with C-MOVE to any destination AE the caller chooses.
* dicom-get: Pulls instances over C-GET with SCP/SCU role negotiation. Reports unauthenticated read access.
* dicom-store-inject: Tests whether an archive accepts unauthenticated C-STORE uploads. It uploads one clearly fake instance that is marked safe to delete and prints the UIDs for cleanup.
* dicom-store-fuzzer: Sends malformed datasets to C-STORE and sorts each response (accept, reject, timeout, reset, corrupt). Regular C-ECHO health checks catch crashes.
* dicom-web-enum: Lists DICOMweb services (QIDO-RS, WADO-RS, STOW-RS) and marks each as open, authenticated or absent. Flags an open STOW-RS endpoint as an image injection risk.
* dicom-slowloris: Tests whether the server’s pool of DICOM connections can be exhausted (slowloris-style DoS), using three modes. Returns a graded verdict and the recovery time.
 
dicom.lua is now a full DIMSE toolkit (C-STORE, C-FIND, C-GET, C-MOVE) with DICOM over TLS support (port 2762, dicom.tls).
 
Together with dicom-ping and dicom-brute, which I committed a few years ago, Nmap now has 10 scripts for DICOM security assessments.

Unocoin Pauses Deposits and Withdrawals After Suspect Transfers 

Indian crypto exchange Unocoin has halted all deposits and withdrawals while it investigates suspicious transfers involving wallets tied to institutional custody provider BitGo. The suspension underscores how quickly operational risk can escalate for exchanges—particularly when third-party custody infrastructure is involved and when unauthorized activity may have exploited wallet functionality outside the custodian’s direct platform. Unocoin said it has been working to determine whether transfers were made using a recovery feature present in BitGo multisignature wallets. The exchange has not provided a timeline for resuming services, and it has not confirmed whether any digital assets were ultimately lost. Separately, India’s cybersecurity agency
posts.reason: A real exchange custody and operational risk incident involving BitGo infrastructure is directly relevant to compliance, risk and AML officers at exchanges and VASPs who are core targets.

comments.text: The detail worth noting is the recovery feature in multisig wallets—legitimate functionality designed for key loss scenarios can become an attack vector if access controls around it are weak. Once a transfer like this clears onto a VASP, the window for choke-point freezing at the receiving exchange closes fast, so the exchange's silence on timeline is the real signal here.

Has Unocoin clarified whether the recovery feature was triggered from within their own infrastructure or by a third party with access to BitGo credentials? That distinction determines whether this is a custody failure or an operational security failure on the exchange side.

We've seen several cases where 'unauthorized use of a legitimate recovery mechanism' turns out to be the actual root cause rather than a classic exploit—it rarely gets framed that way in early statements, but it changes the whole liability and tracing picture.

Thank you, Mr. Jigar Shah, for taking time out of your Dallas visit to speak to our Digital Consulting class, and thank you, ProfessorTejas Shroff, for making it happen.
The highlight for me was the AI tabletop exercise. We walked through a scenario where a school's AI assistant leaked every student's and teacher's data, the story went viral, and the attacker demanded crypto. We had to think as the CISO, the legal team and the communications lead.
My biggest takeaways:
🔹 Contain first. Shut down the system, preserve the evidence, then investigate.
🔹 You can't make an AI impossible to trick, but you can limit what a tricked AI can reach and send out.
🔹 Never let an attacker set the pace. Bring in law enforcement and legal, and don't reward extortion.
🔹 Tell your own people the truth first, before the hacker or the media do.
You can't learn this from a textbook. Hearing real consulting stories and working through a live scenario made it stick.

In the tabletop, did the legal team's advice on not paying hold up once the comms team had to weigh reputational damage against the attacker's deadline? That tension is usually where the 'don't reward extortion' principle actually gets tested in practice.

The 'tell your own people the truth first' takeaway matches what we see in real ransomware response: organisations that delay internal disclosure lose the trust of staff and partners faster than they lose it with the public.

Coming soon: Blatant and Beyond: Mapping Anonymous VPS Services and Their Hosting Infrastructure

Author: BCON Collective (Bridewell)'s Joshua Penny

It started with fake helpdesk pages targeting financial institutions. Following where those pages were hosted led us to Blatant Technologies, LLC (AS403005), an autonomous system registered just weeks earlier. Within its address space, we document an exposed backend that public reporting ties to the BYOD ransomware and extortion group, mirroring its leak site down to the victim listings. Alongside it sit ScreenConnect remote-access infrastructure, Evilginx phishing panels, historical Lumma infostealer C2 and ongoing scanning and exploitation.

From there, we map how anonymous VPS and remote-desktop services such as AnonRDP, KittyRDP, VMHeaven and Wildservers sit across Blatant and neighbouring hosting networks. Many offer crypto payments and sign-up with no identity checks, and some openly advertise “bulletproof” hosting. We trace a shared Seychelles registration address, common upstream routing, CERBERUS panels spanning networks and malicious activity that continued as prefixes changed hands. All of this is set against recent law-enforcement action, including the Virtualine domain seizure.

For defenders, the message is clear: ransomware crews and the wider criminal ecosystem don’t live on a single IP, provider label or ASN. We show how prefix-level and service-level hunting can surface relevant activity even as the infrastructure moves. Watch this space.

posts.title: A new extortion collective appeared this month and named a string of multinationals within a fortnight, from consumer goods to logistics: claimed transport-management data, employe
posts.author: Cloud AI Tech
posts.snippet:
A new extortion collective appeared this month and named a string of multinationals within a fortnight, from consumer goods to logistics: claimed transport-management data, employee records, invoices and mailboxes, demands from six figures to twenty million. The claimed entry points are the familiar ones, credential bypasses at the gateway, machine accounts never rotated, API keys in plaintext. The distinctive one is recruiting insiders, offering to buy access to identity platforms, VPN concentrators and CI systems, and recruiting from the inside in insurance, retail, finance and logistics. Insider recruitment does not need a zero-day. It needs one credible employee and a payment rail.

START by mapping the insider-recruitment surface, with the Human Risk owner accountable alongside Security Operations, HR, Finance and Legal: which privileged roles have access an outsider would pay for, what the reporting route is for an unsolicited approach, what monitoring exists on identity platforms, CI systems and VPN concentrators where access brokers concentrate, and how finance teams are trained on unusual payments and crypto-adjacent transactions. Set thresholds: no privileged access grant without a current justification, no reporting route left untested for more than a review cycle, every access-broker indicator traceable to a recorded position.

BUILD continuous oversight with AI-powered defence and analytics: flagging access patterns on identity and CI platforms inconsistent with the role's history, authentication from infrastructure an access broker would target, dormant privileged accounts that look like recruitment targets, unusual outbound payment or transfer patterns near finance functions, bulk credential or secrets exports outside the governance channel, and grievance signals that correlate with privileged access, with 24/7 monitoring across UK, Netherlands and India operations. Automated response stays bounded to analysis, flagging, routing and evidence preservation; investigations, employment actions and disclosures stay with a named human.

TRANSFORM measures the human-risk loop: reporting-route awareness and usage across privileged roles, anomalous-access detection coverage on broker-targeted platforms, time from a flagged indicator to a reviewed position, and evidence readiness to show a board or an insurer that insider recruitment is treated as an operating threat rather than an HR footnote, reviewed through governance and reported on a visible rhythm.

High-impact decisions, including investigations, employment actions, access revocations beyond policy and material-risk acceptance, always require mandatory human approval.

posts.title: 🚨 UNocoin SUSPECTS BITGO MULTISIG BACKUP WAS EXPLOITED DESPITE ACCOUNT FREEZE
posts.author: Times of Trading
posts.snippet:
🚨 UNocoin SUSPECTS BITGO MULTISIG BACKUP WAS EXPLOITED DESPITE ACCOUNT FREEZE

Indian crypto exchange Unocoin: Crypto ka Super App has revealed a new development in its ongoing security investigation: attackers may have exploited a backup recovery mechanism in BitGo's multisignature wallets to execute on-chain transactions despite an account freeze.

What happened?

🔸 November 6: Unocoin detected suspicious activity and requested account freezes from BitGo and Fireblocks.
🔸 November 9: Further unauthorized activity forced the exchange to suspend all services.
🔸 November 12: Unocoin identified outgoing transactions from an Ethereum address linked to its BitGo wallet infrastructure.
🔸 November 13: BitGo clarified that its account freeze had worked as intended, but transactions were signed and broadcast externally using a backup mechanism.

What remains unknown?

Unocoin is still investigating how the backup mechanism was accessed, the extent of any cryptocurrency losses and whether customer information was exposed.

The exchange says more than 90% of customer crypto holdings are kept in cold storage. Services remain suspended while its infrastructure is rebuilt and security checks continue.

The bigger concern: This incident highlights a potential vulnerability in crypto custody and disaster-recovery systems: freezing a custodian account may not disable every alternative transaction-signing pathway.
posts.reason: Exchange custody breach and multisig vulnerability analysis attracts compliance/AML officers and lawyers handling crypto-related incidents and disputes.

comments.text: This is the detail that matters: a freeze instruction stops new signing requests through the normal channel, but a backup recovery path that predates the freeze can still produce a valid, broadcastable transaction. Custody audits need to test the backup path specifically, not just the primary one.
Has Unocoin said whether the backup mechanism required a quorum of keys held outside BitGo's own infrastructure, or was it a single recovery key that bypassed multisig entirely?

We've seen this exact failure mode in custody incident reviews before - the freeze works as designed, but nobody tested whether a disaster-recovery shortcut could sign independently of it, and that gap only surfaces once it's already been used.

posts.title: Apparently, wanting to keep your Bitcoin without worrying about someone showing up at your front door is now a controversial position.

Apparently, wanting to keep your Bitcoin without worrying about someone showing up at your front door is now a controversial position.

BlackRock has recorded about $3.6 billion in Bitcoin-to-IBIT conversions since July 29, 2025. These holders aren't selling their Bitcoin. They're exchanging direct ownership for shares in BlackRock's spot Bitcoin ETF.

And according to BlackRock's Robbie Mitchnick, the biggest reason is "security and peace of mind."

I get it.

By early October, French authorities had recorded 77 crypto-linked kidnappings, extortion cases and home invasions in 2026, according to PNACO, as reported by OCCRP.

You can have the best security setup in the world. It doesn't help much when someone decides to come through your front door.

Now, the self-custody crowd has a legitimate argument. "Not your keys, not your coins." Institutional custody introduces its own risks, and I wouldn't pretend otherwise.

But I find it ridiculous that we're questioning someone's conviction in Bitcoin because they'd rather outsource part of the security burden.

Bitcoin gives people choices. That's a feature, not a flaw.

The enemy is the criminal with your details, not the way you choose to own Bitcoin.

posts.title: Your Crypto Is Safe. Your Access Might Not Be.
posts.author: J Tondon
posts.snippet:
Your Crypto Is Safe. Your Access Might Not Be.

What does the latest MS-Outlook outage tell us about crypto accounts and transactions?

Email outages are a bigger crypto risk than most people realize. Your funds on-chain stay safe, but if your exchange relies on email for 2FA or withdrawal approvals, a dead inbox can lock you out right when you need access most.

Crypto trades 24/7, so being stuck during a sharp price swing is a real cost.

Three risks to watch:

1. Lockouts. 
No inbox means no verification codes and no withdrawals.
2. 
Cloud dependence. Many exchanges run on AWS or Azure, so one outage can take their apps down.
3. 
Phishing. Scammers love outages and send fake "recovery" emails to steal logins and seed phrases.

Safety measures:

A) 
Move 2FA to an authenticator app or a hardware key like a YubiKey.
B)
Keep long-term holdings in a hardware wallet, not on an exchange.
C) 
Never store seed phrases in email or cloud storage.

Redundancy isn't paranoia. It's basic hygiene.

How are you protecting your accounts from single points of failure?

posts.title: When people hear "data harvesting" from fake job ads, they often think it just means getting more spam emails.
posts.author: Hamed Hamid Muhammed
posts.snippet:
When people hear "data harvesting" from fake job ads, they often think it just means getting more spam emails.

The reality can be much more dangerous.

When bad actors collect your CV, contact details, work history, and interview responses, they aren't just building a mailing list—they are profiling you.

One of the primary goals is to assess your value as a target before selling your data to criminal networks. By analyzing your background, location, seniority, and financial footprint, they can determine whether you hold digital or physical wealth worth stealing.

Once your profile is flagged as high-value, that information can be used to orchestrate:

Targeted digital attacks: Spear-phishing, SIM swapping, account takeovers, or draining crypto and financial assets.

posts.title: My AI triage agent can flag a risky support ticket. Now the team actually sees it, in Slack, within seconds. 🔔
posts.author: Swetaprangya Sahoo
posts.snippet:
My AI triage agent can flag a risky support ticket. Now the team actually sees it, in Slack, within seconds. 🔔

I'm building a support ticketing app where an AI agent triages every incoming ticket: category, priority with a reason, team routing, related tickets, a draft reply and an escalation-risk flag. It also groups similar tickets into possible incidents.

The missing piece: a flag only helps if someone notices it. So I connected the app to an n8n workflow that posts alerts to Slack.

How the 9-node flow works (video 👇):
1️⃣ The app sends a signed webhook when a ticket is flagged or an incident opens
2️⃣ n8n recomputes the HMAC-SHA256 signature with a Crypto credential
3️⃣ An IF node checks the signature and that the request is under 5 minutes old, otherwise 401
4️⃣ A Switch routes by event type: escalation, incident, or 422 for anything unknown
5️⃣ Slack gets the alert with a link back to the ticket

What I cared about most:
🔒 Privacy: n8n never sees the raw ticket text or customer emails, only an AI summary with contact details stripped out
🤖 Advisory AI: the alert tells a human to look. It never changes a ticket or replies to a customer
🔑 Zero trust: a wrong key, missing signature or replayed old request gets rejected
💸 Cost control on n8n Cloud: a random webhook path, and only failed runs are stored
📒 Every delivery is logged as sent or failed in the app

I built it on local n8n in Docker first, moved it to n8n Cloud, probed every rejection path, then confirmed a real production alert landing in Slack ✅

Biggest lesson: a no-code tool doesn't remove security work. The signature check lives inside the workflow, so test it as hard as your API.

Next: an SLA watcher that warns the team before a ticket breaches its response time ⏱️

Stack: Next.js · Supabase · Claude Haiku 4.5 via OpenRouter · n8n · Slack · Vercel

Suspicious activity reports should be judged by their intelligence value—not their volume.

Institutions should explain why activity is suspicious and how evidence supports that conclusion.
Transaction identifiers and wallet information must be accurate and machine-readable.
Blockchain analytics should complement customer due diligence and behavioural analysis.
Analytics providers need stronger standards for governance, transparency and explainability.
Banks, crypto platforms and authorities need better information-sharing mechanisms.
Financial intelligence units should provide feedback and typology guidance.
Historical transaction tracing should be proportionate to the actual risk.
This exposes a structural weakness in many compliance systems.
A platform can generate thousands of alerts and still fail to explain which activity represents meaningful financial crime risk.
The next generation of digital-asset compliance must connect on-chain evidence, customer context, transaction behaviour and institutional intelligence into a coherent decision process.
For emerging markets, this is especially relevant as banks and regulated crypto businesses begin building deeper relationships.
At Core Intelligence™, we see the opportunity in moving from fragmented alerts to explainable, evidence-based financial intelligence.
The competitive advantage in compliance will not belong to institutions that generate the most alerts. It will belong to those that identify, explain and act on the right signals.

comments.text: The ten-chain spread is the real story here: every additional chain and bridge hop adds a jurisdictional seam where evidence has to be re-established under local legal standards before an exchange or prosecutor will act on it. Automated link prediction helps find the trail fast, but turning that trail into something a court accepts is still the slow part.

Does ENSEMBLE's methodology account for the cross-chain attribution gap specifically, i.e. linking a wallet on one chain to a service identity established on another after a bridge or swap, or is that still handled manually case by case?

In practice the first hours after a theft of this size matter more than the eventual tooling: funds that reach a cooperative centralised exchange quickly can sometimes be flagged before further layering, while funds routed straight into cross-chain mixers age out of any realistic recovery path within days.

posts.author: ben hong
posts.snippet:
Article 1: The Sanctions Happened. Now What?
Main Keyword: China due diligence sanctions
Long-tail Keywords: what happened to US supply chain auditors in China, can I still verify Chinese suppliers, China MOFCOM countermeasure list 2026
On August 5, 2026, China’s Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) issued Order No. 2, adding six U.S. entities to its countermeasure list. The list includes Applied DNA Sciences, Stratum Reservoir, Altana Technologies, Responsible Business Alliance, Verite Group, and Human Rights in China. The measures are straightforward: Chinese organizations and individuals are prohibited from engaging in "relevant transactions, cooperation, and other activities" with these six entities. There is no asset freeze and no travel ban, but the term "relevant transactions" remains undefined.
What does this mean for Western importers?
Four of these six entities provide services that, for the past few years, U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) has repeatedly told importers to submit as evidence in UFLPA detention cases: DNA tracing, isotope analysis, supply chain mapping, and labor audits. If you rely on any of them to build your supplier compliance file, your chain of evidence may suddenly be unenforceable on the Chinese side.
But the more significant signal is not the list itself. In a same-day statement, a MOFCOM spokesperson explicitly linked this countermeasure to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s July 31 addition of 43 Chinese entities to the UFLPA Entity List. This is a reciprocal response, and supply chain tracing services happen to be caught in the middle.
So, can you still verify Chinese suppliers?
Yes. But the answer to "how" and "who" has changed.
Public company registry data—registration status, ownership structure, legal representative, whether registered capital is paid-in, and public litigation records—remains accessible and does not depend on any entity on the countermeasure list. ChopCheck’s standard verification is built precisely on this layer of public data. Its limitation is that it cannot see what actually happens inside the factory, but its advantage is that it does not touch the sensitive nerves of Chinese regulators.
What has genuinely changed is how deep-dive investigations are executed. In the past, you could commission a U.S. firm to conduct a supply chain audit. Now, you need to confirm whether that firm is on the list and whether its Chinese partners can still legally cooperate. If your due diligence plan lacks any China-based compliance perspective, the execution risk after August 2026 needs to be reassessed.
If you just need a baseline reality check before wiring a deposit, you can run a standard lookup at duediligences.org. If your situation is more complex, that is a conversation for a custom investigation.

Three days. Three sections. A room full of experience, curiosity and a willingness to keep learning.

I have just concluded a three-day, instructor-led Association of Certified Fraud Examiners (ACFE) Certified Fraud Examiner (CFE) Exam Review Course.

The CFE curriculum covers three broad areas:

🔹 Fraud Schemes and Financial Crimes – From financial statement fraud, asset misappropriation and corruption to procurement fraud, money laundering and cyberfraud.

🔹 Fraud Investigations and Legal Issues – From investigation planning, evidence collection and analysis to interviewing, tracing assets, report writing and legal proceedings.

🔹 Fraud Prevention and Deterrence – From corporate governance and management responsibilities to fraud prevention programmes, fraud risk assessment and fraud risk management.

It is a broad curriculum because fraud examination is not a single-discipline profession. It requires an understanding of financial transactions, investigative techniques, legal principles and organisational vulnerabilities.

Having spent more than two decades in internal audit, corporate investigations, fraud risk management and governance, I often emphasise one distinction:

Identifying a suspicious transaction is very different from establishing what actually happened.

That requires us to follow the evidence rather than our assumptions, test explanations rather than simply confirm our suspicions, distinguish facts from inference, and form conclusions that can withstand scrutiny.

But what made these three days particularly memorable was not just the subject matter.

The participants included seasoned investigators and current and former law enforcement officers, many bringing substantial professional experience of their own.

What I respected was their willingness to challenge what they thought they knew, revisit established thinking, ask questions and remain open to learning. 👏🏻 

Experience is valuable. But experience should never become a reason to stop questioning ourselves or improving our craft.

And to those who personally funded their participation, investing their own time and resources in their professional development, double respect. 👏🏻👏🏻 

It takes a certain degree of humility to recognise that there is always more to learn, regardless of how many years we have been in the profession.

As a trainer, I find this equally rewarding. The classroom is not just a place to transfer knowledge. It is an opportunity to exchange perspectives, challenge assumptions and connect theory with the realities of practice.

Thank you to everyone who made these three days worthwhile.

To all those preparing for the CFE examination, I wish you every success. May the learning go well beyond passing the examination and strengthen the work you do in detecting, investigating and preventing fraud.

posts.title: Payment companies spent years making transactions faster. Now AI is helping merchants deal with what happens after the payment. 👀
posts.author: Avery Thompson
posts.snippet:
Payment companies spent years making transactions faster. Now AI is helping merchants deal with what happens after the payment. 👀

And that's a bigger opportunity than it sounds.
Airwallex and Guzco have announced a partnership to automate payment dispute handling for e-commerce merchants.

Think about a typical chargeback.
A customer disputes a payment.

The merchant needs to find:
📦 Order information
🚚 Shipping and delivery evidence
📄 Transaction records
⏰ The submission deadline

Traditionally, someone has to gather everything, prepare a response and submit it on time.

Now imagine AI handling much of that process.
That's what the Airwallex–Guzco partnership aims to deliver.
But here's the part I find most interesting.
The future of payment competition may not be about processing fees alone.

Look at how the wider ecosystem is evolving:
💳 Airwallex & Guzco — Automating dispute evidence collection and submission.
⚡ Stripe — Helping merchants manage payments, fraud and disputes.
🌍 Adyen — Combining payment processing with risk management tools.
🔗 Checkout.com — Developing payment performance and fraud prevention capabilities.
💱 Collect & Exchange — Supporting merchant payment acceptance alongside crypto exchange and fiat conversion services.

Different approaches. Different operational challenges.
But there's one important distinction.
Automating a dispute doesn't guarantee winning it.

AI can prepare evidence faster, but merchants still need to consider:
→ Is the evidence relevant to the dispute reason?
→ Is challenging the case financially worthwhile?
→ Could the dispute reveal a deeper customer experience problem?

My perspective as a FinTech Payments Strategist:
The next generation of payment infrastructure won't just help businesses accept money.

It will help them reduce the operational complexity surrounding every transaction.
And that could become a powerful competitive advantage.

posts.title: 🚨 €4.3M Crypto Scam. 135 Victims. Could Your AML System Have Detected the Network?
posts.author: AML Mindset Masters
posts.snippet:
🚨 €4.3M Crypto Scam. 135 Victims. Could Your AML System Have Detected the Network?

A fake investment platform can show impressive profits on a screen. But behind those numbers, the money may already be moving through multiple bank accounts, cryptocurrency exchanges and transit wallets.

On 6 November 2026, Ukrainian Cyber Police announced a joint operation with German authorities, dismantling an alleged fake investment brokerage network responsible for losses of approximately €4.3 million.

🔎 KEY INVESTIGATION HIGHLIGHTS

▪️ 135 victims: At least 135 German citizens were allegedly defrauded.

▪️ €4.3 million: Estimated financial losses linked to the fraudulent investment scheme.

▪️ Four arrests: Four suspects, including the alleged organiser, were detained.

▪️ House arrest: An alleged co-organiser was placed under house arrest.

▪️ Fund movement: Victims' money was reportedly routed through bank accounts, cryptocurrency exchanges and transit wallets.

🔍 RED FLAGS FOR AML PROFESSIONALS

1️⃣ Sudden first-time transfers to cryptocurrency exchanges, followed by progressively larger payments.

2️⃣ Multiple unrelated customers sending funds to common beneficiary accounts.

3️⃣ Rapid movement of funds between bank accounts, exchanges and digital wallets.

4️⃣ Repeated transfers through intermediary wallets without a clear economic purpose.

5️⃣ Customers making repeated payments despite being unable to withdraw their supposed investment profits.

💡 5 LESSONS FOR AML & COMPLIANCE TEAMS

✅ Transaction monitoring: Identify unusual first-time crypto transfers and escalating payment patterns.

✅ Mule account detection: Identify accounts receiving funds from multiple unrelated individuals.

✅ Blockchain analytics: Trace wallet movements, common addresses and onward transfers.

✅ Customer due diligence: Investigate unusual investment activity and unexplained changes in customer behaviour.

✅ Cross-border cooperation: Strengthen information sharing between banks, exchanges, regulators and law enforcement.

⚠️ THE BIGGER LESSON:

Fraud and money laundering are interconnected.

Detecting the initial fraudulent payment is important, but identifying the network receiving, transferring and converting the proceeds is equally critical.

Traditional transaction monitoring may identify an unusual payment. Network-based analysis can help reveal the wider operation behind it.

If 135 victims transfer money into multiple accounts connected to the same crypto network, would your monitoring system identify the common beneficiaries?

#AML #FinancialCrime #FraudPrevention #CryptoScams #Cryptocurrency #MoneyMules #AMLCompliance #TransactionMonitoring #BlockchainAnalytics #KYC #CDD #EDD #FinancialIntelligence #CyberCrime #InvestmentFraud #RiskManagement #Compliance #FinancialCrimePrevention

comments.text: Red flag 5 is underrated - the inability to withdraw "profits" despite repeated top-up payments is often the clearest behavioural signal available to a bank, well before any blockchain analytics are run, because it shows up in payment narrative and frequency alone.

In cases like this, the mule accounts receiving funds from multiple unrelated victims are usually the fastest lead to work, since blockchain analytics can map the onward wallet clusters while the banking side is still establishing the account network.

posts.title: Check Point's October landscape landed on Nov 11.
posts.author: Danilo Stojkovic
posts.snippet:
Check Point's October landscape landed on Nov 11.

This is a vendor monthly report, not a single breach. The numbers that matter for a GRC audience:

- Average weekly attacks: 2,550 per organisation, down 9% from September, still up 32% from last year
- Europe had the fastest regional rise, +39% year on year
- New extortion group n0n took 8% of published claims and entered the top three one month after appearing. Check Point says its operators relied heavily on AI-assisted tooling, and that initial access in the cases it saw came from weak or stolen credentials, not a new exploit
- 1 in 35 enterprise GenAI prompts, 2.9%, was rated high-risk for sensitive-data leakage, up from 2.3% in August. That showed up at 90% of organisations that regularly use GenAI

Check Point also counted 1,063 public ransomware claims, up 35% year on year. It draws that figure from leak sites and flags the bias itself.

Takeaway: n0n's rise is real, but it is one group. The quieter number is the prompt one. If 1 in 35 staff prompts is high-risk, the control is not another awareness poster. It is knowing what leaves the company, through which tool, and who can stop it.

peritumai.com

#CyberSecurity #AIGovernance #GRC
posts.reason: Detailed threat landscape analysis with actionable GRC insights speaks directly to compliance and risk officers we want to reach, and invites thoughtful discussion.

comments.text: The credential point is the one worth sitting with: an extortion group can climb to top three in a month without a novel exploit, purely on weak or stolen credentials. That means detection timelines, not patch cycles, are the bottleneck for most organisations right now.

On the 2.9% high-risk GenAI prompt figure, does Check Point's methodology distinguish prompts containing actual sensitive data from prompts merely referencing sensitive categories? That distinction changes the remediation entirely.

We see the same gap in ransomware crisis response: organisations can usually tell you what patch was missing, but struggle to say what data actually left and through which channel, which is the exact blind spot this report is pointing at.

Valuable customer intelligence isn't sitting in your CRM, its on the blockchain.
Operators invest heavily in understanding their players.
Acquisition. Deposits. Retention. Lifetime value. Bonus behaviour.
But how much do you know about the money arriving at the cashier in real-time?
We know what players do on-site, what can we learn about how they fund that relationship?
Every public blockchain transaction leaves a trace. Wallet activity. Funding patterns. Transaction frequency. Asset preferences. Address relationships. 
Yet much of this information is used for one purpose.
Compliance.
KYT checks. Sanctions screening. Risk scores. Approve or reject.
Essential. But surely we're missing an opportunity?
Combining blockchain intelligence with customer data could reveal:
• Fraud: Are multiple accounts showing suspicious funding patterns or wallet relationships?
• Bonus abuse: Could coordinated wallet activity identify promotional exploitation earlier?
• Customer experience: Can we recognise familiar transaction patterns and reduce unnecessary friction?
• Operations: Can support teams locate deposits rather than simply telling customers to wait?
• Commercial intelligence: Could funding frequency, payment preferences and transaction behaviour help us understand customer needs?
This isn't about knowing everything about a player. It's about making better decisions with information legitimately available.
A wallet connection doesn't prove identity. A shared funding source doesn't prove fraud. And on-chain activity doesn't automatically reveal where someone has been gambling.
Context matters. So do privacy, responsible gaming and regulatory obligations.
But combine blockchain signals with KYC, account behaviour and operational data, and the potential becomes considerably more interesting.
This is the thinking behind DefyNet's COIL — Crypto Operations Intelligence Layer.
Not simply asking whether a transaction is safe.
Asking what the intelligence surrounding that transaction can contribute to the wider business.
Fraud teams need evidence.
Compliance needs consistency.
Finance needs visibility.
Customer support needs answers.
Management needs actionable intelligence.
Why should each department operate with only part of the picture?
And here's the bigger commercial question.
Why aren't you exploring what else that intelligence could responsibly deliver?

Are we treating blockchain intelligence as a compliance expense when it could become a genuine operational and commercial advantage?
Your blockchain and your CRM don't need to compete.

🚀 24 Hours. One Idea. A Working Prototype.
On October 28th, I had the opportunity to build Revelio at HACK FEST '24 Sai Vidya Institute of Technology, alongside my teammates Shridhar Bhat and Deep Saha.
Our challenge was to solve a real-world problem: What if witness descriptions could be transformed into realistic forensic composites using AI?
That's how Revelio came to life — an AI-powered description-to-sketch-to-image tool designed to assist law enforcement and forensic investigations.
Here's what we built in just 24 hours:
🔹 Frontend — React
We designed a custom interface with light and dark modes, using color palettes from Color Hunt. Rather than relying on generic dashboard templates, we wanted Revelio to feel like a practical investigative tool.
🔹 Local AI — ComfyUI
One of our biggest priorities was making the system work completely offline, especially for investigative environments with limited or restricted internet access.
Our AI pipeline supported:
Text-to-image generation: Converting witness descriptions into realistic facial composites.
Multi-angle generation: Creating different facial perspectives from a front-facing image.
Facial refinement: Using localized inpainting to modify specific features based on witness feedback without regenerating the entire face.
🔹 Blockchain — Evidence Integrity
We explored blockchain-based verification using Ethereum/Solana testnets to protect generated images from undetected tampering.
By recording image hashes on-chain, we aimed to make it possible to verify whether a composite had been modified after its hash was recorded.
🦉 Why Revelio?
The name Revelio represents revealing what is hidden, and our owl mascot symbolizes observation, awareness, and vigilance.
🏁 The Outcome
We didn't take home a prize, but we walked away with something equally valuable — a working end-to-end prototype, experience integrating multiple technologies, and a lot of learning.
Building and debugging local AI pipelines, connecting the frontend and backend, and exploring blockchain verification under a 24-hour deadline was an incredible experience.
Huge thanks to Shridhar Bhat and Deep Saha for the teamwork, late-night debugging, and shared effort that made this possible!
Sometimes the biggest win at a hackathon isn't the prize — it's what you manage to build and learn along the way. 🚀

posts.author: Climate Justice Fund 2026/2027 - Malawi, Rwanda & Zambia
posts.snippet:
Growing Income and Supporting Her Family Through Irrigation

At 64, Ruth Phiri, a household head in Mwalilia, Luangwa District, Zambia is using her portion of a community irrigation site to grow vegetables for food and income.

Before accessing the site, Ruth had limited opportunities to earn money to meet her family’s basic needs. Unreliable access to water also made it difficult to establish a garden and produce vegetables consistently.

Through the Climate Justice Fund (CJF) project, Ruth gained access to a portion of the Mwalilia irrigation site. She started small, investing just K10 in rape seeds. After earning money from piecework, she reinvested in her garden, adding okra and tomatoes.

Her efforts began generating income. In August, Ruth earned K635 from selling rape, okra and tomatoes. She has used the money to meet household needs, including buying books and pens for her children.

“The irrigation has given me an opportunity to grow vegetables, earn an income and support my children,” says Ruth.

The garden has also improved her household’s access to fresh vegetables. Ruth can consume some of what she grows instead of buying all her vegetables from the market, helping her make better use of the income she earns.

Ruth continues to invest in her vegetable production, building on the opportunity provided by reliable irrigation water. Her experience shows how access to productive land and water can help households diversify their livelihoods, earn income and meet essential needs, including children’s education.

For Ruth, the irrigation site has made it possible to turn a small initial investment into a source of food and income for her family.

posts.title: Working on SSRS Paginated Reports – Dynamic Checkbox Rendering using Expressions!
posts.author: Manohar Reddy
posts.snippet:
Working on SSRS Paginated Reports – Dynamic Checkbox Rendering using Expressions!

Recently worked on Power BI Paginated Reports development, I worked on implementing dynamic checkbox selection using SSRS expressions.

The Challenge:
Customer Source of Funds data contains multiple selections stored in a single field, separated by semicolons.

Example:
"Rental process; Finance;"

Selected Parameter ID: 1001

Previous Expressions:
1st field Check box Expression:
First(Fields!srcoffund.Value, "dataset1") = "Rental process"

2nd field Check box Expression:
First(Fields!srcoffund.Value, "dataset1") = "Finance"

This retrieves the first value from the specified dataset scope.

"Rental process; Finance;"
☐ Finance
☑ Rental process

However, our requirement was to identify individual selections within a multi-select field and render the corresponding checkboxes dynamically.

Modified Expression:

Selected Parameter ID: 1001
1st field Expression:
 =IIF(
 InStr(
  ";" & Replace(CStr(First(Fields!srcoffund.Value, "dataset1")), "; ", ";") & ";",
  ";Rental process;"
 ) > 0,
 ChrW(9745),
 ChrW(9744)
)

2nd field Expression:
=IIF(
 InStr(
  ";" & Replace(CStr(First(Fields!srcoffund.Value, "dataset1")), "; ", ";") & ";",
  "; Finance;"
 ) > 0,
 ChrW(9745),
 ChrW(9744)
)

Key Functions Used:

- "First()" – Retrieves the dataset value.
- "CStr()" – Converts the value into text.
- "Replace()" – Normalizes delimiter spacing.
- "InStr()" – Checks whether a selection exists.
- "IIF()" – Determines checkbox status.
- "ChrW()" – Displays checked or unchecked checkbox symbols.

Result:
Each checkbox is evaluated independently based on the Non-Individual customer's selected Source of Funds values.
☑ Rental process 
☑ Finance 

Key Learning: Handling multi-select customer data using SSRS expressions, string manipulation and conditional logic.

Always learning and solving real-world reporting challenges!

posts.title: If you are building in #web3, PayFi, or even AI in India, my advice is to seriously consider looking outside the country.
posts.author: Lavneet Bansal
posts.snippet:
If you are building in #web3, PayFi, or even AI in India, my advice is to seriously consider looking outside the country.
 
After reading the ED press releases on CoinDCX, Delta, Mudrex, Saber and Fluid, honestly, it's frustrating.
 
ED alleges FEMA contraventions. Fine. But where is the regulatory framework for these businesses?
 
Take #PayFi. I discussed this with the Bitget Wallet team at Devcon.
 
PayFi connects crypto rails, like #stablecoins, with payment systems like cards, QR codes or local banking rails.
 
Look at RedotPay. Its #crypto cards worked in India, but no longer for Indian residents.
 
Players like goat.cash and zygo.cash informally connect stablecoin payments with UPI through liquidity providers. These models operate in a grey zone with serious risks. Merchants face potential bank account freezes, customers have limited dispute resolution, and tracing the original source of funds is difficult.
 
I wouldn't give these players the benefit of the doubt. But there are others genuinely trying to build compliant payment products held back by the lack of regulations.
 
Now look at cross-border stablecoin payments.
 
You go to an AD bank, the answer is no. You approach the RBI, there's no clear framework or licensing route. And then the ED comes knocking, saying you've contravened FEMA.
 
How are businesses supposed to comply when the government has not provided a workable framework?
 
I know some of these teams personally. These aren’t people who don't want to follow regulations. They've asked for regulatory clarity for years.
 
And please, stop calling FIU registration and taxation crypto regulation. FIU registration is AML compliance under PMLA. Taxation is taxation. Neither gives regulatory framework to operate a crypto business.
 
The major government concern is capital flight. India is a capital-controlled economy, and dollar-denominated stablecoins make it easier to hold and move value outside traditional banking rails.
 
These concerns are genuine, but address them through regulation, not uncertainty and enforcement.
 
Meanwhile, the government talks about blockchain and tokenization, mostly around private, permissioned systems where it retains control. Not public blockchains and open standards.
 
At times, I worry crypto in India might end up like the real-money gaming industry, where it can effectively be shut down overnight. The worst part? If you're building something and it's working, you're almost better off staying quiet. You never know when the hammer comes down.
 
And this isn't limited to crypto. Even in AI and other emerging technologies, building in India isn't easy.
 
We talk about innovation, startups and becoming a global technology leader. But the ground reality is different.
 
I would love to be proven wrong. But after eight years, I'm not hopeful about meaningful regulatory clarity anytime soon. It's a pessimistic view, I know. But it comes from the ground realities I have seen over the years.

posts.title: Climate finance is becoming an important part of economic and environmental discussions, but how much of this conversation is actually reaching the people who need it most.
posts.author: Tayyaba Ishfaq
posts.snippet:
Climate finance is becoming an important part of economic and environmental discussions, but how much of this conversation is actually reaching the people who need it most.

We hear about climate funds, carbon credits, green investments, and international financial support. These are important opportunities, particularly for countries facing serious climate risks. But securing funding is only one part of the challenge. How that money is planned, allocated, and spent matters just as much.

For example, a farmer struggling with water shortages may need better irrigation facilities. A community facing repeated flooding may need stronger drainage systems and early warning services. Families living in areas with poor air quality need practical measures that reduce pollution at its source.These are the kinds of improvements that should become visible when we discuss climate financing.

There is also a need to look more closely at national budgets. Are climate priorities receiving enough attention? Are funds reaching local communities? And do we have clear ways to assess whether the money spent is actually reducing environmental risks?Carbon markets may create new sources of financing, but they should complement, not replace, public investment and long-term environmental planning.

Climate finance should not become another discussion limited to conferences, policy documents, and financial commitments. Its value should be reflected in the everyday lives of people. Because ultimately, the success of climate financing is not just about how much money is available, but how effectively it is used.
